title: Greek Colonies
capsule: The term 'Greek Colonies' encompasses the network of apoikiai (settlements) planted by poleis across the Mediterranean and Black Sea littorals from the eighth to fourth centuries BCE, reaching peak density by the classical period. The Cliopatria dataset window of c. 271–225 BCE captures the late Hellenistic phase, when most colonies had matured into independent or semi-autonomous cities and many had passed under Macedonian, Ptolemaic, or Seleucid overlordship. Massalia (Marseille), founded c. 600 BCE by Phocaea, and Neapolis (Naples), Cyrene, and Olbia are among the most significant foundations. The colonial network was progressively absorbed by Rome, Carthage, and successor kingdoms through the third and second centuries BCE.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. As an aggregate entity spanning hundreds of individual settlements, territorial extent is inherently approximate; individual colony sites are well attested archaeologically but the collective polygon is a scholarly construct.
